evidence: Histories of early Detroit techno equipment routinely name the Mirage as shared among Saunderson, May and Atkins in the mid-1980s. The sourcing is secondary rather than first-person, so this is consensus.

earlier.title: Mirage, an eight-bit sampler at 1,695 dollars

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen to how the record is put together underneath the vocal: short stabs that all stop dead rather than ring out, repeating in the same place every bar. Then notice what the sampler let him do that the others could not, which is put a full sung performance on top of it. Detroit techno arriving on daytime radio starts here.

explanation.age7: The same cheap sampling keyboard turned up on a record that became a big pop hit.
explanation.age13: Saunderson used the same kind of cheap sampler as his friends in Detroit, but he put a proper sung vocal over the top of it and made records that got played on the radio. The machine was noisy and could only hold a couple of seconds at a time, which is why the sounds all stop abruptly instead of ringing out.
explanation.adult: Included partly to show the same tool producing a different commercial outcome in the same city and social circle, which is an argument against technological determinism even in a project that gives machines their own nodes. Consensus tier: the equipment attribution is secondary sourcing.
